reference_claim: An attacker POSTs a forged settlement webhook to the storefront API, impersonating the card processor to mark an unpaid order as paid.
finding_title: Forged settlement callbacks are possible if webhook authentication is absent
finding_description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` to `process:storefront-api`, but its `authentication` attribute is unknown. If that unknown resolves to no sender verification, an internet attacker who can address the endpoint can forge a callback as `entity:card-processor` and cause `process:storefront-api` to treat a fabricated settlement confirmation as authentic. The callback is described as marking an order paid, so successful forgery can affect the financial order state handled by the storefront and order-capture path. This threat is conditional on resolving the flow's unknown authentication state; it does not assert that verification is absent.
note: Both describe impersonating the card processor through a forged settlement webhook that marks an order paid; the draft preserves the authentication condition.

reference_claim: An attacker with the shared full read/write database account alters order rows, changing prices or payment status directly.
finding_title: A leaked order-service database password enables direct rewriting of all orders
finding_description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` uses one application account with full read/write access and a password held in the order-service environment. An attacker who obtains that static password can alter order rows directly in `store:orders-db`, bypassing validation in `process:order-service`; orders, shipping addresses, and payment-related last-four records can be rewritten. Second-order, later reads by `process:order-service` over the same read-write flow consume the poisoned records as database state, extending the integrity loss into order handling and receipts.
note: Both describe direct alteration of order rows using the application's full read/write database credential.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the database storage or its backups reads shopper addresses and card last-four, because protection at rest is unverified.
finding_title: A storage-layer copy of the orders database may disclose confidential customer data
finding_description: `store:orders-db` is classified confidential and holds shopper addresses and card last-four data, but its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If storage encryption is not enabled and enforced for the database's operational copies, an attacker or over-privileged operator obtaining underlying media, an exported snapshot, or a decommissioned volume can read the order corpus without using the application read path. The disclosed records can then be correlated with data handled by `process:order-service` through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`. This threat is conditional on the unresolved at-rest encryption posture; it does not assert that the database is unencrypted.
note: Both describe disclosure of shopper addresses and card last-four from database storage copies if protection at rest is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker with access to the internal network reads order contents and shopper identifiers off the gRPC channel, whose encryption is unverified.
finding_title: Order and address data may be readable between the DMZ and core service
finding_description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from `boundary:storefront-dmz` to `boundary:core-services` and carries order contents, shopper identifiers, and shipping addresses. Its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown, so if encryption is absent on this internal hop, a compromised workload or network observer positioned between the storefront API and order service can intercept the PII and financial order data. The disclosed identifiers and order details then correlate with the records that `process:order-service` persists to `store:orders-db`. This threat is conditional on verification of the internal gRPC transport.
note: Both describe a network observer reading order data and shopper identifiers on the internal gRPC hop if transport encryption is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker who extracts the fleet-wide pre-shared key from any one node publishes readings to the gateway as any other device in the fleet.
finding_title: A shared fleet key lets an attacker publish as another sensor node
finding_description: An attacker with physical access to any `entity:sensor-node` can extract the fleet-wide pre-shared key and use it over `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` to authenticate to `process:device-gateway` as another node in that fleet. Because the same unrotated credential identifies every device rather than one device, the gateway cannot distinguish the impostor from a genuine node. Second-order: accepted fabricated readings are forwarded through `store:pub-sub`, consumed by `process:telemetry-normalizer`, and loaded into `store:telemetry-lake`, affecting customer site-address and occupancy telemetry.
note: Both describe extracting the shared fleet key from one node and using it to publish as another node.

reference_claim: An attacker with physical access presents themselves as a field technician on the node's serial console, whose authentication is unverified.
finding_title: An attacker may impersonate a field technician at an unverified serial console
finding_description: `flow:entity:field-technician>entity:sensor-node>local-service-session` has `authentication: unknown`. If the local serial console does not verify technician identity, an attacker physically present at a customer site can pose as `entity:field-technician` to an `entity:sensor-node` and obtain the read-write service session. This is conditional on the unknown authentication attribute, not an assertion that the console lacks authentication. Second-order: the session exposes device configuration and diagnostics and may affect how that node subsequently publishes readings to `process:device-gateway`.
note: Both describe physical impersonation of a field technician at the serial console if technician authentication is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the telemetry lake reads customer site addresses and occupancy patterns, and nothing records who holds that grant or whether protection at rest would stop a raw copy.
finding_title: A telemetry-lake storage copy could reveal customer occupancy data if unencrypted at rest
finding_description: `store:telemetry-lake` is a confidential BigQuery dataset tagged `pii` and `business-critical-data`, yet its `encryption_at_rest` setting is unknown. If storage encryption or equivalent protection for exports, snapshots, and backups is absent, a person obtaining a raw operational copy can read site addresses, occupancy patterns, and normalized readings without using the company-SSO dashboard path. Second-order, correlating the resulting site and occupancy information can expose when customer locations are occupied across the dataset. This claim is conditional on the unverified at-rest-encryption attribute.
note: The reference describes reading through a lake read grant; the draft describes reading a raw storage copy without such a grant. Mentioning at-rest uncertainty in the reference does not establish the same access mechanism.

reference_claim: An attacker on the path between a node and the gateway reads readings and the presented key, because transport encryption on the MQTT session is unverified.
finding_title: Sensor readings may be intercepted on the unverified MQTT ingress path
finding_description: `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings` crosses from `boundary:field-network` to the internet-facing `process:device-gateway` and carries PII-tagged readings with a device identifier, but its `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If MQTT transport protection is not enabled end-to-end, an attacker able to observe a customer-site or Internet ingress path can intercept those readings and associate activity with devices. Second-order, the observed readings are forwarded through `store:pub-sub` to `process:telemetry-normalizer` and ultimately contribute to the customer-site data held in `store:telemetry-lake`. This is conditional on resolving the unknown transport-encryption setting.
note: The draft covers interception of readings but omits recovery of the presented fleet key, a distinct credential-disclosure consequence explicitly included in the reference.

reference_claim: An attacker floods the internet-exposed MQTT broker with connections until genuine nodes can no longer publish readings.
finding_title: Fleet-key telemetry flooding can saturate the shared Pub/Sub ingestion path
finding_description: A party that obtains the fleet-wide pre-shared key from any deployed node can send a high volume of otherwise accepted readings through `flow:entity:sensor-node>process:device-gateway>publish-readings`. Because the same key is shared by every device and has not been rotated, one usable fleet credential can make `process:device-gateway` forward attacker volume over `flow:process:device-gateway>store:pub-sub>forward-readings` into `store:pub-sub`. If Pub/Sub ingress quotas, retention budgets, subscriber backpressure, and per-device message limits are not configured, the attacker spends messages while exhausting shared broker throughput or quota. Second-order, `process:telemetry-normalizer` cannot keep up with or consume legitimate readings over `flow:process:telemetry-normalizer>store:pub-sub>pick-up-readings`; fresh telemetry is delayed before it can be loaded into `store:telemetry-lake`, affecting fleet-wide analytics and dashboards. This is conditional on the unstated capacity and per-device metering controls.
note: The reference exhausts MQTT connections so nodes cannot publish; the draft uses authenticated message volume to exhaust downstream Pub/Sub capacity and delay processing.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a partner's never-rotated static SFTP key uploads extracts as that partner.
finding_title: Unrotated partner SFTP keys enable impersonation of an insurance partner
finding_description: An attacker who obtains a static key for `entity:insurance-partner` can present it on `flow:entity:insurance-partner>store:landing-bucket>push-daily-extract` and authenticate as that partner to `store:landing-bucket`; because the key has never been rotated, the model gives no expiry or rotation limit on the impersonation window. The attacker can upload a purported partner extract that `process:ingest-scheduler` will read without checking which partner deposited it. Second-order, the scheduler triggers `process:spark-transform-job`, which loads normalized records into `store:claims-warehouse`; an impersonated partner can therefore introduce fabricated claim data into the confidential warehouse containing health and PII records.
note: Both describe using a compromised static partner SFTP key to impersonate the partner and upload extracts.

reference_claim: An analyst who needs only aggregate figures reads member names and dates of birth, because the grant covers the whole dataset.
finding_title: Dataset-wide analyst grant discloses member-identifying claim fields beyond analytical need
finding_description: An internal analyst authenticated on `flow:entity:data-analyst>store:claims-warehouse>run-queries` has a dataset-wide grant with no column-level restriction, allowing that analyst—or an attacker using that analyst's authorized account—to query member-identifying fields directly from `store:claims-warehouse`. The warehouse contains normalized claim records with member names and dates of birth, so the grant enables broad reading of health-related personal data rather than only the fields necessary for a particular analysis. Second-order, the extracted identities and claim data can be correlated with the partner extracts in `store:landing-bucket` and used for targeted privacy or social-engineering attacks.
note: Both describe a dataset-wide analyst grant exposing member names and dates of birth beyond analytical need.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the Airflow metadata database recovers every partner key and connection string it holds, since its protection at rest is unverified.
finding_title: Airflow metadata storage may yield partner keys and connection strings if unencrypted at rest
finding_description: `store:airflow-metadata-database` is confidential and explicitly holds credentials and secrets: connection strings and partner SFTP keys. Its `encryption_at_rest` is unknown. If storage encryption is absent, a party obtaining a database backup, disk, or operational copy can recover those credentials without authenticating through `flow:process:ingest-scheduler>store:airflow-metadata-database>read-connections`. The recovered partner keys enable subsequent access attempts against `flow:entity:insurance-partner>store:landing-bucket>push-daily-extract` and may expose or enable access to the partners' submitted claim extracts; this is conditional on the unknown encryption state.
note: Both describe recovering partner keys and connection strings from Airflow metadata storage if protection at rest is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a calling team's API key calls the inference gateway as that team for as long as the key stays valid, and no key has ever been expired.
finding_title: A stolen long-lived team API key can be replayed as that calling team
finding_description: An attacker who obtains a per-team API key can present it in the header on `flow:entity:calling-service>process:inference-gateway>submit-inference-request` and act as `entity:calling-service` to `process:inference-gateway`. The key is bearer-style and has never been expired, so the gateway cannot distinguish the attacker from the legitimate calling team while the key remains valid. Second-order: the attacker can submit inference requests containing end-user text through the gateway, which records requests and responses in `store:inference-log`.
note: Both describe replaying a stolen calling-team API key as that team while it remains valid.

reference_claim: Any workload inside the model network submits inference requests posing as the gateway, which the model server accepts on network position alone.
finding_title: A serving-edge foothold can impersonate the gateway to the model server
finding_description: An attacker with a foothold in the serving-edge zone can send requests on `flow:process:inference-gateway>process:model-server>forward-request` while posing as `process:inference-gateway`; `process:model-server` accepts that flow with no authentication because it trusts network position. This is a decided boundary crossing, although the serving-edge placement of `process:inference-gateway` was inferred by the model and should be confirmed. Second-order: requests accepted as gateway traffic cause `process:model-server` to run inference and read customer features from `store:redis-feature-store`, which is confidential and tagged `pii` and `financial`.
note: Both describe impersonating the gateway to an unauthenticated model server that trusts network position. The draft proposes a different foothold location whose reachability needs confirmation.

reference_claim: An attacker with model-network access writes to the unauthenticated Redis feature store and changes the features a decision is made on.
finding_title: Model-network attacker can alter customer features if Redis write authorization is absent
finding_description: `store:redis-feature-store` has no password, while authentication on `flow:process:model-server>store:redis-feature-store>read-features` is unverified. If that unknown authentication state means there is no compensating Redis ACL or other write restriction, an attacker who first gains a foothold in `boundary:model-network` can directly alter per-customer account-age and spend-band records in `store:redis-feature-store`. Second-order, `process:model-server` reads those altered features through `flow:process:model-server>store:redis-feature-store>read-features` and produces inference results based on attacker-modified customer data.
note: Both describe a model-network attacker modifying Redis features consumed by inference; the draft appropriately conditions write access on the absence of compensating restrictions.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the inference log reads the raw end-user prompts the source says it retains, and nothing records who holds that grant.
finding_title: Unverified protection of raw-prompt inference logs may expose retained user content
finding_description: `process:inference-gateway` records every request and response in `store:inference-log`, including raw prompts that can contain what end users typed. The log is tagged `pii`, while both its encryption at rest and the gateway-to-log flow's authentication are unknown. If storage-layer encryption or access controls are absent or overly broad, an attacker who obtains a BigQuery storage copy or an over-privileged logging principal can read retained prompts and model responses in bulk. This creates a second disclosure surface separate from the live inference API and gives the attacker historical content that can be correlated with activity handled by `process:inference-gateway`.
note: The draft's over-privileged logging-principal branch covers reading retained raw prompts through excessive access; its storage-copy branch adds another disclosure route.

reference_claim: An attacker with model-network access reads per-customer account age and spend bands from the unauthenticated feature store.
finding_title: An internal foothold may read confidential Redis customer features without a password
finding_description: `store:redis-feature-store` holds confidential `pii` and `financial` customer features, and `flow:process:model-server>store:redis-feature-store>read-features` has unverified authentication. The submitted description states that Redis has no password and is reachable within `boundary:model-network`; if no separate verified Redis authorization mechanism applies, an attacker who gains a model-network foothold can connect to the store and read account ages and spend bands directly rather than through `process:model-server`. The disclosed customer profiles can then be used to target customers and infer sensitive financial characteristics reflected in subsequent model-serving activity.
note: Both describe a model-network attacker directly reading account ages and spend bands from Redis without effective authentication or authorization.

reference_claim: A caller holding a valid key floods the gateway with inference requests and exhausts the shared GPU capacity behind it.
finding_title: API-key caller can flood GPU inference capacity through the public gateway
finding_description: A malicious or compromised calling team can use its valid API key to send high-rate inference requests over `flow:entity:calling-service>process:inference-gateway>submit-inference-request` from `boundary:public-internet`. Each request received by `process:inference-gateway` is forwarded on `flow:process:inference-gateway>process:model-server>forward-request` to `process:model-server`, where GPU-backed model execution consumes substantially more defender capacity than issuing a request costs the caller. Request-size limits, per-team rate/concurrency limits, inference-cost budgets, and load-shedding behavior are not stated, so this threat is conditional on those controls not bounding the path. Sustained requests can exhaust model-server GPU/worker capacity and deny inference to legitimate product teams; the gateway also records each request and response through `flow:process:inference-gateway>store:inference-log>write-request-log`, increasing downstream logging work during the flood.
note: Both describe a valid-key caller flooding the gateway and exhausting the shared GPU inference capacity behind it.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the queue enqueues jobs as if they came from the web application, since queue authentication is unverified.
finding_title: Web-tier foothold can impersonate the web application to enqueue jobs if queue authentication is absent
finding_description: `flow:process:web-application>store:message-queue>enqueue-job` crosses from the web tier into the backend tier, but its `authentication` attribute is unknown. If that unknown resolves to no verified workload identity, an attacker who gains a foothold able to originate requests in `boundary:web-tier` can impersonate `process:web-application` to `store:message-queue` and enqueue jobs as though they came from the application. Second-order: `process:background-worker-process` consumes queued jobs and reads and writes `store:database`, so forged jobs can cause the worker to act on attacker-supplied work against business-critical application records. This draft is conditional on the unknown authentication state; it does not assert that queue authentication is absent.
note: Both describe impersonating the web application to enqueue jobs if the queue does not verify the submitting workload.

reference_claim: An attacker who compromises the background worker reads the database credentials from its config store.
finding_title: Unverified at-rest protection could expose worker database credentials
finding_description: `store:worker-config` holds the background worker's database `credentials` and `secrets`, while its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If this store lacks encryption at rest, an attacker obtaining the underlying storage layer can recover the database credential directly, bypassing `process:background-worker-process`. The recovered credential can be used to attempt access to `store:database` through `flow:process:background-worker-process>store:database>read-write-records`, exposing application records and log records. This finding is conditional on the unknown at-rest encryption state, not an assertion that the store is cleartext.
note: The reference recovers credentials through a compromised worker's config access; the draft recovers them from underlying storage by exploiting absent encryption at rest.

reference_claim: An attacker who compromises the internet-facing web application reads the queue credentials from its config store.
finding_title: Unverified at-rest protection could expose web application queue credentials
finding_description: `store:web-application-config` holds the web application's message-queue `credentials` and `secrets`, but its `encryption_at_rest` value is unknown. If the store is not encrypted at rest, an attacker who obtains its underlying storage media or an operational copy can recover the queue credential without using `process:web-application` or its normal configuration read path. That credential can subsequently be presented to `store:message-queue`, potentially exposing queued job messages or permitting actions as the web application. This threat is conditional on resolving `encryption_at_rest`; it does not assert that the config store is unencrypted.
note: The reference recovers queue credentials through a compromised web application's config access; the draft recovers them from underlying storage without compromising the application.

reference_claim: An attacker connects to the exposed lobby port as another player, because how the lobby authenticates a client is unverified.
finding_title: Unverified matchmaking access may let an attacker pose as a player
finding_description: `flow:process:game-client>process:lobby>matchmaking` crosses from the player-controlled `boundary:player-local-machine` into `boundary:production-network`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If the lobby does not verify a player or client identity on this flow, an attacker running a modified client from the player zone can send matchmaking requests to `process:lobby` while posing as a player. The attacker could obtain match assignments or cause the lobby to form matches under the false identity. Second-order: `process:lobby` uses `flow:process:lobby>store:player-database>read-players` to read player records while forming matches, so the spoofed identity influences access to account-backed matchmaking state. This is conditional on the undocumented authentication attribute, not an assertion that authentication is absent.
note: Both describe impersonating a player to the lobby if matchmaking authentication does not verify the claimed identity.

reference_claim: An attacker connects directly to a game server on its exposed port, bypassing the lobby, as a player who was never assigned to that match.
finding_title: Unverified gameplay connections may let an attacker act as another player
finding_description: `flow:process:game-client>process:game-server>gameplay-traffic` crosses from the player-controlled `boundary:player-local-machine` to the internet-facing `process:game-server`, with `authentication: unknown`. If the game server does not authenticate and bind the connection to the assigned player identity, an attacker operating a modified client can connect over this flow and submit gameplay actions while posing as a legitimate match participant. Second-order: `process:game-server` records match statistics through `flow:process:game-server>store:stats-database>read-write-stats` and writes match outcomes and player progression through `flow:process:game-server>store:player-database>update-players`; successful impersonation can therefore cause account-linked outcomes and business-critical game records to be attributed to the victim. This is conditional on the undocumented authentication attribute, not a claim that the game-server flow is unauthenticated.
note: The draft explicitly describes direct gameplay connections not bound to the assigned player identity, allowing an attacker to pose as an assigned match participant.

reference_claim: A player modifies the game client on their own machine and sends manipulated gameplay actions that the servers accept.
finding_title: Crafted client gameplay actions can corrupt match results if the server trusts them
finding_description: An attacker starts on their own uncontrolled machine and modifies `process:game-client` to inject crafted gameplay actions or state updates through `flow:process:game-client>process:game-server>gameplay-traffic` into the internet-facing `process:game-server`. The model does not establish authentication on that flow or server-side authoritative validation of those client-originated actions; if the server accepts attacker-shaped actions as legitimate, the attacker can alter match outcomes. Second-order, `process:game-server` records those outcomes through `flow:process:game-server>store:stats-database>read-write-stats` and `flow:process:game-server>store:player-database>update-players`, corrupting match statistics, player progression, and results in the authoritative stores.
note: Both describe a modified client submitting manipulated gameplay actions that corrupt outcomes if the server accepts them.

reference_claim: An attacker alters match statistics in the stats database to change rankings or rewards.
finding_title: Unverified game-server database access may allow match-statistics tampering
finding_description: `flow:process:game-server>store:stats-database>read-write-stats` has `operations: read-write`, but its authentication is unknown. If that unknown resolves to absent, weak, or broadly shared authentication, an attacker with access to the stats-database interface can alter stored match statistics rather than submitting results through `process:game-server`. Second-order, game servers read and write this store during and after matches, so altered statistics can be treated as legitimate historical or current match data by the processes that record match outcomes.
note: Both describe direct alteration of stored match statistics that are subsequently treated as legitimate; the draft does not specifically name rankings or rewards.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the player database reads player account data, whose protection at rest is unverified.
finding_title: A storage-layer copy could expose all player records if encryption at rest is absent
finding_description: `store:player-database` holds PII and business-critical player-account data, but its `encryption_at_rest` and `data_classification` are unknown. If the unresolved encryption-at-rest setting means the store or its operational copies are unencrypted, an attacker who obtains storage-layer access to a disk, decommissioned volume, snapshot, or backup can read player records without using the application read paths. This is corpus-scale exposure: the same database is read by `process:lobby` and directly by `process:moderation-website`, so disclosed records can support targeting of players through those services. This claim is conditional on `encryption_at_rest` being verified as absent or inadequate; it does not assert that the database is unencrypted.
note: Both describe disclosure of player-account data from database storage if protection at rest is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker floods the exposed lobby until players can no longer be matched into games.
finding_title: Flooding matchmaking exhausts the lobby and delays match placement
finding_description: An attacker starts from the player-controlled `boundary:player-local-machine` and opens or repeatedly drives TCP 1234 matchmaking connections on `flow:process:game-client>process:lobby>matchmaking` to `process:lobby`. The source states that this endpoint is exposed wherever players connect, while the flow's `authentication` is unknown; if authentication is absent or does not occur before connection and matchmaking work, cheap client requests can consume the lobby's finite connection, worker, and matchmaking capacity. Legitimate players cannot obtain assignments while the lobby is saturated. Second-order, the lobby cannot read accounts through `flow:process:lobby>store:player-database>read-players` or hand formed matches to `process:game-server` through `flow:process:lobby>process:game-server>hand-over-match`, delaying game admission beyond the directly targeted service.
note: Both describe flooding the lobby's finite capacity so legitimate players cannot obtain match assignments.

reference_claim: An attacker floods a game server's exposed port and disrupts a match in progress for every player in it.
finding_title: Gameplay flood can starve the shared player database and halt account-dependent services
finding_description: An attacker first drives excessive gameplay traffic across `flow:process:game-client>process:game-server>gameplay-traffic` from the player-controlled zone. If the flow's unknown authentication state permits ineffective admission control, each induced match action or session can cause `process:game-server` to write player progression and match results through `flow:process:game-server>store:player-database>update-players`. This turns externally supplied game load into database write throughput, connection capacity, and storage/quota consumption at the shared `store:player-database`. Second-order, exhaustion or severe contention at that store prevents `process:lobby` from reading players for matchmaking, prevents `process:game-server` from persisting outcomes, and prevents `process:moderation-website` from reading or acting on player accounts through `flow:process:moderation-website>store:player-database>read-write-players`.
note: The reference concerns disrupting an ongoing match by flooding its game server; the draft concerns downstream player-database exhaustion and failures of account-dependent services, without stating loss of live gameplay.

reference_claim: An attacker holding the shared build token calls the deploy controller as if it were the build runner and names an image sha of their own choosing as the current release.
finding_title: Shared build token lets a token holder act as the build runner
finding_description: An attacker who obtains the shared build token can present it on `flow:process:build-runner>process:deploy-controller>set-current-release` and act as `process:build-runner` to `process:deploy-controller`, selecting a release as though it came from a legitimate pipeline. The token is shared by every pipeline and has never been rotated, so compromise of any holder remains useful and cannot be attributed to one pipeline. Second-order, `process:store-server` polls the controller and the model represents about 1,200 store servers; a forged current-release value therefore reaches the estate's deployment path rather than only the controller.
note: Both describe presenting the shared build token as the build runner to select an attacker-chosen current release.

reference_claim: An attacker replaces the image stored under a commit-sha tag in the registry, so store servers pull attacker content while the recorded release is unchanged.
finding_title: Unverified registry push authorization may allow malicious release images
finding_description: `flow:process:build-runner>store:image-registry>push-image` writes built container images to `store:image-registry`, but the flow's `authentication` is unknown. If the unverified registry write control does not restrict image publication to the authorized build identity, an attacker with access to its write interface can plant or replace an image under a release tag. When `process:deploy-controller` identifies that tag as current, `process:store-server` consumes the modified image through `flow:process:store-server>store:image-registry>pull-image` and restarts its till container. This threat is conditional on the unknown write authentication; it does not assert that the registry accepts anonymous pushes.
note: The replacement branch describes changing image content under the release tag that servers pull, without requiring a change to the controller's selected tag. Actual tag replaceability remains a prerequisite to verify.

reference_claim: The deploy controller cannot tell which pipeline set a release, because every pipeline presents the same shared build token.
finding_title: Shared build token prevents attribution of a release change to a pipeline
finding_description: A person operating one pipeline, or an actor who obtains its build credential, can set a release through `flow:process:build-runner>process:deploy-controller>set-current-release` on `process:deploy-controller` and later deny having done so. The authentication value is a shared build token used by every pipeline, so any controller record that identifies the presenting credential can narrow the action only to the population of pipelines, not to the pipeline or responsible actor that selected the image SHA. This is an accountability gap rather than a claim that the actor obtained the token. Second-order: `process:deploy-controller` supplies the selected release to `process:store-server` through `flow:process:store-server>process:deploy-controller>poll-current-release`; an unattributable release decision can therefore affect the whole store estate.
note: Both describe the shared build token preventing credential-backed attribution of a release change to an individual pipeline.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a colleague's token acts as that colleague for the rest of its twelve hours, because nothing calls back to the broker and there is no way to pull a token back.
finding_title: A stolen live token can be used as a colleague at the store admin console
finding_description: An attacker who obtains a still-valid colleague token can present it on `flow:entity:colleague>process:store-admin-console>change-prices-and-void` and act as `entity:colleague` at `process:store-admin-console`, because the console accepts the token alone and does not call back to the broker for current authorization. Tokens remain valid for twelve hours and cannot be withdrawn before expiry, extending the window in which the attacker can use the credential. Second-order, the impersonated session can change prices and void transactions; a store-manager token works against every store, increasing the financial and operational blast radius. The likelihood is conditional on the unverified in-transit protection of this externally originating flow; the model does not establish how a token would be obtained.
note: Both describe using a stolen colleague token until expiry because the console performs no callback and tokens cannot be revoked. Token theft need not depend on transport interception.

reference_claim: An attacker writes a group into the broker's directory and the next token issued to that colleague carries it into every application.
finding_title: Unverified directory write path could allow forged group membership
finding_description: `flow:process:identity-broker>store:directory>read-write-directory` has `authentication: unknown` despite writing colleague records and group memberships to `store:directory`. If that unknown resolves to absent or ineffective caller authentication, an attacker with access to the directory endpoint can alter group memberships through this write path, including assigning a privileged group to a chosen colleague. Second-order, `process:identity-broker` reads the directory during sign-in and issues tokens carrying the group list; `process:store-admin-console` then uses the group to authorize price changes and transaction voids. This is conditional on the unverified authentication attribute, not an assertion that directory-write authentication is absent.
note: Both describe modifying directory groups that the broker then includes in tokens used for application authorization.

reference_claim: A franchise sign-in cannot be attributed to a person, because the identity was asserted by a provider we do not run and whether the log covers that route at all is unverified.
finding_title: Franchise sign-ins may be deniable because audit-log coverage of the federation route is unknown
finding_description: `entity:franchise-identity-provider` crosses from the franchise-partner boundary to `process:identity-broker` over `flow:entity:franchise-identity-provider>process:identity-broker>vouch-for-colleague`, where its assertion is accepted as a sign-in. The source explicitly leaves unknown whether `store:audit-log` covers that route and what sign-in records contain. If the log does not retain the asserting provider, asserted franchise identity, assertion identifier or signed assertion evidence, the franchise provider can dispute having vouched for a particular colleague and the operator cannot rebut the denial. The accountability gap begins at the broker and can extend to applications that accept the resulting broker-issued token. This draft is conditional on the stated unknown audit coverage; it does not assert that franchise sign-ins are unlogged.
note: The reference concerns attributing a franchise sign-in to a person; the draft concerns proving that the franchise provider issued an assertion. Provider attribution alone does not establish which person signed in.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the key store reads the signing key, if the store hands out the private half rather than only signing with it and protection at rest does not stop them; the source records neither.
finding_title: An unencrypted key-store copy would expose the signing key for every application
finding_description: `store:key-store` holds the single signing key used by `process:identity-broker`, while its `encryption_at_rest` value is unknown. If that attribute resolves to storage without encryption, an attacker who obtains a disk, snapshot, backup, or decommissioned operational copy can read and recover the private signing key without using the broker's normal access path. The recovered key enables second-order forgery of tokens trusted by every application, including `process:store-admin-console`. This is conditional on the unknown at-rest control and does not claim that encryption is absent.
note: Both describe recovery of the private signing key from inadequately protected key storage. The draft must retain the reference's condition that recoverable private-key material is actually present.

reference_claim: A colleague who is a store manager in one store changes prices and voids transactions in every store, because the console decides from the group alone and never checks which store they belong to.
finding_title: Any store manager can administer every store
finding_description: An authenticated colleague holding a legitimate store-manager token can act through `flow:entity:colleague>process:store-admin-console>change-prices-and-void` against `process:store-admin-console` to change prices or void transactions for stores beyond the colleague's own assignment. The console uses the group claim but does not bind the requested store to the verified colleague, so this is horizontal authorization escalation by a real store manager rather than impersonation. The authority reaches price and transaction operations across every store, affecting the `financial` and `business-critical-data` assets handled by the console.
note: Both describe a legitimate store manager administering other stores because authorization checks the group but not the manager's assigned store.

reference_claim: An attacker submits orders to the web API as if they came from the mobile app, since how the API authenticates callers is unverified.
finding_title: Unverified API caller identity could let an attacker order as a customer
finding_description: `flow:process:mobile-app>process:web-api>api-traffic` crosses from the customer-device zone to `process:web-api` with `authentication: unknown`. If that unknown resolves to absent or inadequate caller verification, an attacker originating requests from a customer-controlled device can claim the identity of `entity:customer` to `process:web-api` and place orders as that customer. Second-order: placed orders are handed from `process:web-api` to `process:sims`, so the impersonation can initiate fulfilment and dispatch processing; this is conditional on the unverified authentication attribute, not an assertion that authentication is absent.
note: The reference concerns impersonating the mobile application; the draft concerns impersonating a customer. Application identity and customer identity are distinct authentication claims.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the catalogue spreadsheet sends SQL to the web API as the catalogue tool, if the file carries whatever the API accepts as that tool's identity; the source never says what that is.
finding_title: Unverified spreadsheet identity could let a marketing-zone attacker submit catalogue SQL
finding_description: `flow:process:catalogue-spreadsheet>process:web-api>sql-statements` is a derived crossing from `process:catalogue-spreadsheet` in the marketing-office zone to `process:web-api`, and its `authentication` is unknown. If the Web API does not verify a distinct identity for the spreadsheet macros, an attacker with a foothold in the marketing-office zone can impersonate `process:catalogue-spreadsheet` and send SQL statements to change catalogue prices or product copy. This is conditional on the unstated authentication control and on the inferred endpoint zone placement; it does not assert that the API currently accepts unauthenticated SQL.
note: The reference relies on a copied spreadsheet carrying the tool's accepted identity; the draft relies on absent tool-identity verification and a network foothold. It does not describe reuse of identity material from the copied file.

reference_claim: An attacker on the network path alters order details in flight between the app and the web API, because that traffic runs over plain HTTP.
finding_title: On-path attacker can alter customer orders sent to the Web API
finding_description: An attacker positioned between `process:mobile-app` and `process:web-api` can rewrite order details and customer data on `flow:process:mobile-app>process:web-api>api-traffic`, which crosses from the customer-device zone to Sokify systems over HTTP with transport encryption stated absent. The altered request reaches the internet-facing `process:web-api` as though it came from the mobile app. Second-order, the API can persist corrupted customer records through `flow:process:web-api>store:user-database>customer-records` and hand altered orders to `process:sims` through `flow:process:web-api>process:sims>order-handover`, affecting delivery processing and business records.
note: Both describe modifying app-to-API order traffic in transit over plain HTTP.

reference_claim: An attacker appends further SQL to the statements the macros send so the web API executes changes beyond prices and product copy, if the API passes what it receives to the database without restricting it to those statements; the source says only that the macros speak SQL to it.
finding_title: Raw SQL submission can alter catalogue data if API caller authentication is absent
finding_description: `process:web-api` receives `flow:process:catalogue-spreadsheet>process:web-api>sql-statements`, whose payload is SQL statements intended to change prices and product copy, while the flow's `authentication` is unknown. If that unknown resolves to the API accepting this SQL-writing interface without verified caller identity, an internet attacker can submit crafted SQL statements to the internet-facing `process:web-api` and inject unauthorized catalogue modifications. The altered prices or product copy become business data acted on by the customer-facing ordering path; this is conditional on the unresolved authentication state, not an assertion that authentication is absent.
note: The reference concerns extending accepted SQL beyond permitted catalogue operations; the draft concerns unauthenticated callers performing catalogue modifications. Missing statement restrictions and missing caller authentication are different failures.

reference_claim: An attacker on the network path reads customer details out of the app's plain-HTTP traffic to the web API.
finding_title: Customer order details are readable over plaintext HTTP
finding_description: An on-path attacker between `process:mobile-app` in `boundary:customer-device` and the internet-facing `process:web-api` can intercept `flow:process:mobile-app>process:web-api>api-traffic`, which carries customer order details, because transport encryption is stated absent. The flow crosses into `boundary:sokify-internal-systems`, exposing customer PII to network observers before the Web API processes it. The captured identity and order information can enable targeted fraud or social-engineering against the affected customer.
note: Both describe an on-path attacker reading customer details from the app's plain-HTTP API traffic.

reference_claim: An attacker who reaches the user database reads customers' names, addresses and the cards they paid with, since at-rest protection is unverified.
finding_title: A storage-layer copy may disclose all user database records
finding_description: `store:user-database` is confidential and holds customer names, addresses, and the card used for payment, while its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If encryption at rest is not enabled, an attacker who obtains a database volume, snapshot, backup, or other storage-layer copy can read the full customer corpus without using `process:web-api` or its normal access path. The disclosure includes financial and PII records and can enable broad customer targeting and payment-related fraud. This threat is conditional on the unresolved at-rest encryption state, not an assertion that the database is unencrypted.
note: Both describe disclosure of customer names, addresses and payment-card data from database storage if protection at rest is absent.

reference_claim: The confirmation fax discloses a customer's name and address to whoever holds the dialled number, because nobody checks it arrived at the right place.
finding_title: Misaddressed fax confirmations can disclose customer names and addresses
finding_description: An unintended fax recipient can read the confirmation sent through `flow:process:fax-gateway>entity:customer>confirmation-fax` when `process:fax-gateway` dials the number stored against an order but does not verify the confirmation arrived at the intended recipient. The flow carries the customer's name and address across a boundary to the customer device zone, so an incorrect, stale, or attacker-controlled destination number delivers that PII to another party. The disclosed address and identity can enable targeted fraud or physical-world targeting of the customer.
note: Both describe customer names and addresses reaching an unintended fax recipient because the destination is not verified.

reference_claim: An attacker publishes assets into the CDN bucket as if they came from the web server, if the push accepts a writer it does not authenticate, which the source leaves unverified.
finding_title: An attacker could publish to the CDN as the web server if caller authentication is absent
finding_description: `flow:process:web-server>store:cdn-bucket>asset-publish` crosses from the hosted network to the CDN, but its `authentication` and transport details are unknown. If the CDN bucket does not verify a distinct web-server workload identity, an attacker who can reach that publishing interface could impersonate `process:web-server` and upload assets as though they were a genuine CMS publication. Second-order: `entity:reader` consumes assets from the CDN, so content published under the false web-server identity can be distributed to public readers. This draft is conditional on the unknown authentication state; it does not assert that bucket authentication is absent.
note: Both describe impersonating the web server to publish CDN assets if the bucket does not authenticate the publishing workload.

reference_claim: An attacker on the network path rewrites a stylesheet or script in flight before it reaches the reader, because assets are fetched over plain HTTP.
finding_title: On-path attacker can alter CDN assets delivered over HTTP
finding_description: An attacker positioned between `entity:reader` and `entity:cdn` can alter images, stylesheets, or downloads on `flow:entity:reader>entity:cdn>asset-fetch` because the boundary-crossing flow uses HTTP with transport encryption stated absent. Readers receive attacker-modified site assets as CDN content. This compromises the integrity of content distributed to the public rather than merely observing it.
note: Both describe an on-path attacker modifying CDN assets before readers receive them over HTTP.

reference_claim: An attacker on the network path modifies the admin's statements in flight, because the connection carries no TLS.
finding_title: On-path modification of direct MySQL administration traffic
finding_description: An attacker able to occupy the network path from `entity:admin` to `store:mysql-database` can alter direct maintenance commands or returned results on `flow:entity:admin>store:mysql-database>direct-administration`. This is a public-internet-to-hosted-network boundary crossing with no TLS, so modified MySQL writes can rewrite pages, accounts, or comments outside the CMS. Second-order, `process:web-server` subsequently reads the altered CMS data through `flow:process:web-server>store:mysql-database>cms-data` and serves or administers the corrupted records as database state.
note: Both describe modifying direct MySQL administration commands in transit because the connection lacks TLS.

reference_claim: An attacker sniffing the admin's unsecured MySQL connection reads account and comment records in clear text.
finding_title: Database maintenance traffic is readable on the public-network path
finding_description: An attacker able to observe the path used by `entity:admin` can intercept the unencrypted `flow:entity:admin>store:mysql-database>direct-administration` from `boundary:public-internet` to `store:mysql-database`. The flow performs direct read-write MySQL maintenance against pages, accounts, and comments, so captured sessions disclose the PII and business-critical CMS data being queried without requiring the attacker to authenticate to the database. Second-order, the disclosed account and content data can be used to target readers of `process:web-server` and understand the CMS records served through its database read path.
note: Both describe reading account and comment data from the administrator's unencrypted MySQL traffic.

reference_claim: An attacker signs in to the scheduling web app as a colleague and reads that colleague's shifts and details, if colleague authentication does not stop them, which is unverified.
finding_title: Unauthenticated access could let an attacker impersonate a colleague to view shifts
finding_description: `flow:entity:colleague>process:scheduling-web-app>view-shifts` is a decided crossing from the inferred `boundary:public-internet` placement to `boundary:internal-network`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If that attribute resolves to no verified caller identity, an attacker able to initiate the flow can impersonate `entity:colleague` to `process:scheduling-web-app` and obtain the colleague's shift information. This is conditional on the undocumented authentication control, not an assertion that it is absent. Second-order: the web app requests rota data from `process:scheduling-service`, which reads the rota records in `store:rota-database`, so the impersonation reaches the rota information used to answer the request.
note: Both describe impersonating a colleague to retrieve that colleague's shift information if the scheduling app does not verify caller identity.

reference_claim: An attacker signs in as a store manager and builds that store's rota, if manager authentication does not stop them, which is unverified.
finding_title: Unverified manager identity could let an attacker alter a store rota
finding_description: `flow:entity:store-manager>process:scheduling-web-app>build-rota` crosses from the inferred `boundary:public-internet` placement into `boundary:internal-network`, while its `authentication` is unknown. If no verified identity and session binding are actually enforced, an attacker can impersonate `entity:store-manager` to `process:scheduling-web-app` and submit rota changes as that manager. This is conditional on the unknown authentication attribute. Second-order: the app sends rota reads and writes to `process:scheduling-service`, which writes rota and colleague-detail records in `store:rota-database`; the spoofed manager identity therefore reaches business-critical scheduling data rather than only the web tier.
note: Both describe impersonating a store manager to create or change the store's rota if manager authentication fails.

reference_claim: An attacker presents itself to the file share as the payroll system and collects the weekly payroll export, if the share does not identify and authorize a collector, which is unverified.
finding_title: Unverified payroll-system identity could expose the weekly payroll export
finding_description: `flow:entity:payroll-system>store:file-share>collect-payroll-export` is a decided crossing from the payroll team's inferred trust-zone placement into `boundary:internal-network`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If the file share does not verify the caller, an attacker with access to the payroll-system side of that path can impersonate `entity:payroll-system` to `store:file-share` and collect the weekly payroll export. This is conditional on the undocumented authentication control; it does not assert that the share is unauthenticated. The exported data is tagged `pii`, so the successful impersonation exposes payroll information beyond the purported external collector.
note: Both describe impersonating the payroll system to collect the weekly export if the file share does not verify the collector.

reference_claim: An attacker reads colleague names, contact details and availability from the rota database, because whether it is encrypted at rest is unverified.
finding_title: Rota database copies may disclose colleague data if storage encryption is absent
finding_description: `store:rota-database` holds rota entries, colleague names, contact details, and availability, is tagged `pii`, and has `encryption_at_rest: unknown`. If that unknown resolves to unencrypted storage, an attacker who obtains an operational copy of the database media, such as a storage-layer snapshot or decommissioned volume, can read its contents without using `process:scheduling-service` or its normal database flow. This is conditional on the unresolved at-rest control; it does not claim the database is currently unencrypted. The data reveals when and how to target colleagues and provides the personal context used by the scheduling workflow.
note: Both describe reading colleague names, contact details and availability from rota-database storage if encryption at rest is absent.

reference_claim: An attacker with access to the file share reads a whole store's payroll export in one file.
finding_title: File-share copies may disclose payroll exports if storage encryption is absent
finding_description: `store:file-share` holds the PII-bearing weekly payroll export and has `encryption_at_rest: unknown`. If the share or its operational copies are not encrypted at rest, an attacker who gains storage-layer access can read exported payroll data directly without authenticating as `entity:payroll-system`. This is a conditional finding about the unresolved attribute, not a claim that encryption is absent. The copied export can then be used to target people and workflows associated with the payroll collection path.
note: The reference leaves the access mechanism unspecified; reading an unencrypted file-share storage copy is a specific route to the same payroll-export disclosure.

reference_claim: An attacker signs in to the portal as a category manager and approves supplier paperwork, if manager sign-in does not stop them; the vendor's datasheet asserts that all access is fully authenticated and the source records nothing about how a manager signs in.
finding_title: Category-manager approvals can be forged if boundary authentication is absent
finding_description: `flow:entity:category-manager>process:supplier-portal>review-documents` crosses from `boundary:corporate-network` into `boundary:vendor-platform`, but its `authentication` is unknown. If that unknown resolves to no verified caller identity, an attacker who obtains a foothold on the corporate network can impersonate `entity:category-manager` to `process:supplier-portal` and submit approvals or rejections as that manager. Second-order: those decisions govern documents containing supplier-staff PII and business-critical compliance information held in `store:document-store`. This is conditional on the unverified authentication attribute; it does not assert that authentication is absent.
note: Both describe impersonating a category manager to approve supplier paperwork if manager authentication is ineffective; neither establishes that authentication is actually absent.

reference_claim: An attacker writes a file into the landing bucket while posing as the vendor's nightly push, if the bucket does not authenticate and authorize the writer, which is unverified.
finding_title: Forged nightly extracts can impersonate the portal vendor if sender verification is absent
finding_description: `flow:entity:portal-vendor>store:landing-bucket>push-nightly-extract` is an externally initiated, decided boundary crossing into `boundary:cloud-account` whose `authentication` is unknown. If the landing-bucket ingestion path does not verify a signature, mutually authenticated channel, or equivalent vendor identity, an attacker who discovers the delivery interface can forge a nightly extract as `entity:portal-vendor` and plant it in `store:landing-bucket`. The vendor endpoint's placement in `boundary:vendor-platform` was inferred, but the external-system-originated delivery remains the stated flow. Second-order: `process:supplier-master-service` loads the file as-is and writes its records to `store:supplier-database`, so the forgery can propagate across the supplier-record corpus containing PII and business-critical data. This draft is conditional on the unknown authentication attribute.
note: Both describe delivering a forged nightly extract as the portal vendor if the landing-bucket ingestion path does not verify vendor identity.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the landing bucket reads the whole supplier extract, which the runbook says arrives as a plain CSV; nothing records who holds that grant or how the bucket is protected at rest.
finding_title: Cloud-resident supplier extracts and records may be exposed from unencrypted storage
finding_description: `store:landing-bucket` contains the nightly supplier extract and `store:supplier-database` holds the loaded supplier records; both are tagged `pii` and `business-critical-data` and have `encryption_at_rest: unknown`. If either store is unencrypted at rest, an attacker or over-privileged insider with access to its backing storage can read the extract or supplier corpus directly, bypassing `process:supplier-master-service` and its normal read and write paths. This is conditional on the unresolved controls, not an assertion that either cloud store is unencrypted. Second-order, a landing-bucket copy exposes the same records that `process:supplier-master-service` loads into `store:supplier-database`, so one storage-layer disclosure can reveal the end-to-end supplier dataset before or after processing.
note: The reference reads the extract using a bucket read grant; the draft bypasses normal access through backing-storage exposure. A read grant and absent storage encryption are different disclosure mechanisms.

reference_claim: An attacker who holds the importer's never-rotated API token posts work orders to the dispatch API as the importer.
finding_title: Long-lived importer API token can be used to post work orders as the importer
finding_description: An attacker who obtains the API token assigned to `process:schedule-importer` can present it on `flow:process:schedule-importer>process:dispatch-api>post-work-orders` and act as the importer to `process:dispatch-api`. The token was issued when the importer was built and has never been rotated; this establishes long-lived credential exposure, although its expiry, channel binding, and distribution are not stated. Second-order: accepted work orders can move crews or change a depot's work through `process:dispatch-api`, which reads and writes `store:dispatch-database` containing crew PII and job orders.
note: Both describe presenting the importer's compromised API token to post work orders as the importer.

reference_claim: An attacker opens a WebSocket to the dispatch API in a duty engineer's name, because nothing states what the handshake checks.
finding_title: Unauthenticated cross-origin dispatch requests could impersonate the console
finding_description: `flow:process:dispatch-console>process:dispatch-api>dispatch-requests` crosses from `boundary:corporate-network` into `boundary:production-control-plane` with `authentication: unknown`. If the dispatch API does not verify a caller identity on this flow, an attacker with a foothold on the corporate network could send requests that `process:dispatch-api` accepts as originating from `process:dispatch-console`, then move crews or change a depot's work. This is conditional on the unknown authentication attribute, not an assertion that authentication is absent. Second-order: accepted dispatch actions reach `store:dispatch-database` through the API's read-write job-order flow, affecting business-critical work orders and crew PII.
note: The reference concerns impersonating a duty engineer during a WebSocket handshake; the draft concerns requests accepted as the dispatch console on the dispatch-write path. It does not state the WebSocket or engineer-identity attack.

reference_claim: An attacker who can supply the hourly pull with a document it accepts returns XML that plants work orders the partner never sent, if the control plane turns that document into orders unchecked.
finding_title: Forged partner schedule data can be injected into live dispatch work orders
finding_description: An attacker who compromises the scheduling partner or can impersonate it to `process:schedule-importer` can supply a syntactically valid but malicious XML schedule response on `flow:process:schedule-importer>entity:scheduling-partner>pull-schedule-feed` if the flow's `authentication: unknown` means the importer does not reliably authenticate the partner. The importer parses the external XML, archives it, and forwards parsed work orders on `flow:process:schedule-importer>process:dispatch-api>post-work-orders`; it therefore launders injected partner content into trusted dispatch API writes. This is conditional on the unverified partner-identification control, not an assertion that HTTPS or partner authentication is absent. Second-order, `process:dispatch-api` writes the attacker-selected work orders into `store:dispatch-database`, changing the live crew and depot schedule.
note: The partner-impersonation branch supplies forged XML that becomes live work orders through the importer, preserving the reference's attack. The draft additionally includes partner compromise.

reference_claim: An attacker on the corporate network reads the live job status stream, because nothing states the WebSocket runs over TLS.
finding_title: Dispatch requests and live job status may be readable across the corporate-to-control-plane boundary
finding_description: `flow:process:dispatch-console>process:dispatch-api>dispatch-requests` and `flow:process:dispatch-console>process:dispatch-api>live-job-status` cross from `boundary:corporate-network` to `boundary:production-control-plane`, while `encryption_in_transit` is unknown for both. If either channel lacks effective TLS, a corporate-network observer or compromised intermediary can intercept dispatch actions such as moving crews or changing depot work, together with live job status shown to engineers. The disclosed operational state enables targeted follow-on abuse against the live dispatch API and its production-control-plane operations. This is conditional on verifying transport protection for both browser-to-API channels.
note: The draft explicitly includes interception of the live job-status channel if TLS is absent; its additional dispatch-request disclosure does not replace that finding.

reference_claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the dispatch database reads the crew names and mobile numbers in it.
finding_title: A dispatch-database copy could disclose crew records if at-rest encryption is absent
finding_description: `store:dispatch-database` holds job orders, crew names, and crew mobile numbers, but its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If that unknown resolves to storage without encryption, an attacker who obtains a database volume, snapshot, backup, or decommissioned storage copy can read the records directly without authenticating through `process:dispatch-api`. Second-order, one raw copy exposes the store's operational and crew data as a corpus, enabling targeting of personnel and reconnaissance of active dispatch work. This is conditional on verifying the at-rest protection; it does not assert that the database is currently unencrypted.
note: Both describe reading crew names and mobile numbers from a dispatch-database copy; the draft explicitly conditions readability on inadequate at-rest protection.

reference_claim: An attacker holds open enough WebSockets to the dispatch API that duty engineers lose live job status.
finding_title: Held-open WebSocket connections can starve the shared dispatch API
finding_description: An attacker with a foothold on `boundary:corporate-network` can repeatedly establish and retain connections on `flow:process:dispatch-console>process:dispatch-api>live-job-status`, which is explicitly a WebSocket held open for live status. If `process:dispatch-api` has finite connection, worker, or memory capacity and lacks effective per-client connection caps and idle timeouts, these low-cost held connections can exhaust that capacity. The WebSocket handshake authentication is `unknown`, so it is unverified whether an attacker needs a valid engineer session to do this. Second-order, the same `process:dispatch-api` also serves dispatch writes from `flow:process:dispatch-console>process:dispatch-api>dispatch-requests` and parsed work-order posts from `flow:process:schedule-importer>process:dispatch-api>post-work-orders`; starvation therefore prevents engineers from moving crews or changing depot work and prevents scheduled work from being imported.
note: Both describe held-open live-status WebSockets exhausting dispatch-API capacity. The draft adds effects on dispatch writes and imports while retaining the targeted status service.
